opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the rabbit example comes from our work on planning in poems. We'd give the model a couplet where the first line ends with something like "grab it," and before it even starts writing the second line, you can see it's already activated features representing candidate rhyming words, like "rabbit" and "habit." So it's planning ahead: it picks the destination and then writes a line that gets there.

When we intervene on that rabbit feature, say we suppress it, what we're changing is the model's internal representation of its plan. We're not editing the output token directly. We're reaching into the middle of the computation and removing the concept it was steering toward. What's striking is that the model doesn't just break. It goes to its next option, "habit," and writes a coherent line ending in "habit." And if you inject a totally different concept, like "green," it'll restructure the whole line to land on "green," even though that doesn't rhyme anymore.

So I think about it as editing a goal rather than a word. The feature sits upstream of a bunch of downstream decisions, like which words to pick earlier in the line and how to set up the syntax, and all of those reorganize around whatever you put there. That's really the evidence that it's a plan and not just a correlation. If the feature were just a byproduct, changing it wouldn't propagate like that.

I'd add a caveat, though. Features are our interpretation of directions in the model's activations, and our replacement models don't capture everything. So when we say "we turned off rabbit," what we really did is perturb a direction we've labeled rabbit, and we check that the effect matches the label. The fact that the downstream behavior changes in such a sensible, predictable way is what gives us confidence the label is meaningful. But we try to stay humble about how clean those concepts are inside the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes suppressing or perturbing a rabbit-labeled direction, but does not say it is subtracted from what the MLP would otherwise write during the forward pass.

r002.rationale: It says suppressing rabbit leads the model to its next option, “habit,” and to write a coherent line ending with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's easy to get sloppy with the language here. When we say we "intervene on the rabbit feature," what we literally do is pretty mundane. We have a replacement model, a sparse representation of the network's activations, and in that representation there's a direction that fires when the model is thinking about rabbits. And when we intervene, we're adding or subtracting some multiple of that direction from the residual stream at a particular layer, at a particular token position, and then letting the rest of the computation run.

So the honest answer to "what are you changing" is: you're changing a vector in the middle of the network. That's it. Everything else is interpretation.

Now, the reason it feels like more than that is because of what happens downstream. In the poetry example, where the model is planning a rhyme and we see the rabbit feature light up at the end of the first line, if we suppress it the model goes and writes a line that ends in "habit" instead. If we inject a different concept, say "green," it rewrites the line to end on green. And so the intervention is doing something that looks like it's at the level of a plan, not just at the level of the next token. That's what makes it interesting.

But I try to hold a couple of things in mind. One is that the feature is a description of a computation, not the computation itself. The model doesn't have a rabbit variable sitting in memory. It has a bunch of superposed directions that we've factored in a particular way, and the factorization could have been different. So when I steer on it, I'm reaching into a lossy approximation and hoping the real network responds the way the approximation says it should. Often it does, and that's actually the main evidence that the approximation is any good. The interventions are the test. If you suppress the rabbit feature and nothing changes, you've learned that your story about what it was doing was wrong.

The other thing is that you're never changing just one thing. That direction participates in a lot of circuits. So when you knock it out, you're also perturbing whatever else was reading from it, and you can get side effects that have nothing to do with rabbits. Part of the methodology is checking that the effect you see is the specific one you predicted, rather than just "the model got confused because I added noise."

So I'd say the mental model is less like flipping a switch and more like nudging a variable in a program you only partially understand, then watching very carefully to see what breaks and what doesn't. And the fact that the nudges are so often clean and targeted tells you something real about how the model is organized. But the clean story is the thing you earn after the experiment, not the thing you get to assume going in.

r001.rationale: It says the intervention subtracts the rabbit direction from the residual stream, but does not say it subtracts a direction from what the MLP would otherwise write.

r002.rationale: It states that suppressing the rabbit feature makes the poem line end in “habit.”

astra-6.text:
I think of it as changing a particular direction in the model’s internal representation, rather than editing a fact in a database. We call it the “rabbit feature” because it seems to activate on rabbit-related inputs. But that label is our interpretation; it doesn’t guarantee that we’ve isolated precisely the human concept of a rabbit.

When we intervene, we’re asking a causal question: if we increase or decrease this feature’s activation, how does the model’s behavior change? Does it become more likely to mention rabbits, or interpret something ambiguous as rabbit-related? Those effects help us understand what the feature does. So I’d distinguish between identifying something that correlates with rabbits and demonstrating that changing it actually influences the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It describes changing a rabbit-associated feature’s activation, but does not say the intervention subtracts that direction from what the MLP writes during the forward pass.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a planned poem ending or redirecting it to “habit.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as changing an internal representation, rather than changing a particular word. So if we identify a feature that seems to respond to rabbits, we can intervene on that feature—turn its activation up or suppress it—and see how the model’s behavior changes.

The interesting question is whether that change generalizes. Does it only make the model say “rabbit” more often, or does it also affect how it talks about related ideas, or how it responds to a rabbit in a different context? That gives us evidence about what the feature is doing. But “rabbit feature” is our shorthand for what we observe; it doesn’t mean we’ve found a perfectly isolated, human-like concept of a rabbit inside the model.

r001.rationale: It describes turning down a feature’s activation, but does not say a rabbit-associated direction is subtracted from what the MLP writes during the forward pass.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible behavioral changes generally; it does not mention a poem ending or the alternative rhyme word “habit.”
